title: Study Shows Where in Lungs Vapes' Toxic Metals Go
paragraphs: According to the World Health Organization, more than 100 million people around the world — including at least 15 million children — use e-cigarettes.

E-cigarettes and vaping are often marketed as a safer alternative to cigarettes. However, not only do they still contain addictive nicotine, but research has found that they may leave toxic metals in users' lungs.
Some of these metals are in the liquid used to give e-cigarettes their flavor, but some also come from the heating elements that turn those liquids into a vapor.
In a study in Analytical and Bioanalytical Chemistry, researchers exposed mice to e-cigarette vapor twice a day over four days to better understand how metal builds up in a user's lungs.
The mice were divided into three groups, receiving the equivalent of eight, 16 or 32 vaping puffs in each session. A fourth group only breathed normal air.

The device the researchers used to produce the vapor had a nickel-chromium heating element. They used a commercially available vape liquid, which they analyzed and found also contained those two metals, as well as zinc, aluminum, copper, lead, mercury and more.
After four days of breathing the vapor, the researchers examined the mice's lungs, using a laser-based imaging system to map exactly where the metals had settled.

They found that different metals tended to build up in different places. Lead and nickel settled more in the upper area of the lungs, as well as in the outer lining. Zinc was found in higher concentrations at the bottom of the lungs.

There was evidence of metal in the lungs of all the mice that were exposed to the vapor. For mice in the 32-puffs group, lead concentrations were 25 times higher than among the mice that just breathed normal air.

Many of the metals left by vaping are linked to health risks. For example, nickel may damage the cells lining the airways. And lead can be absorbed into the bloodstream, spreading to bones, the brain and other organs, where it may contribute to high blood pressure and cognitive problems.
